title: How the statements link
objectives: Answer out loud: Walk me through how the three statements link.
Answer out loud: Why does AR going up reduce cash?
Answer out loud: How do you treat a gain on sale?

steps.body: Net income from the IS is the first line of the CFS.
CFO adds back non-cash items (D&A, SBC, impairments), subtracts non-cash gains, and adjusts for changes in working capital.
CFI: CapEx, acquisitions, asset sales, investments.
CFF: debt raised/repaid, stock issued/repurchased, dividends.
Net change in cash flows to the BS cash line. Net income (less dividends) flows to retained earnings.
The BS balances because every change on one side is matched elsewhere.

legend.meaning: Retained earnings (equity on the balance sheet)

blocks.template: An increase in an operating asset (e.g., AR) is a {{1}} of cash
An increase in an operating liability (e.g., AP) is a {{1}} of cash
Retained earnings = beginning RE + net income − {{1}}

blocks.title: “Walk me through how the statements link.”
blocks.body: **Interview answer:** "Net income from the income statement flows to the top of the cash flow statement and into retained earnings. On the CFS, you add back non-cash expenses, adjust for working capital, then add investing and financing activities to get the net change in cash, which flows to cash on the balance sheet. PP&E, debt, and equity on the balance sheet are also updated from the CFS, and the balance sheet balances."

blocks.title: Why does an increase in accounts receivable reduce cash?
blocks.teaser: AR rising means you recorded revenue (boosting net income) but haven't collected the cash.
blocks.body:
AR rising means you recorded revenue (boosting net income) but haven't collected the cash. The CFS starts from net income, so it must subtract the uncollected amount.

**Interview answer:** "Net income already counts that revenue, but the cash hasn't arrived, so we subtract the increase."

blocks.prompt: Accounts receivable increases by $10. What's the effect on the cash flow statement?

options.text: No effect — AR is on the balance sheet only

blocks.explanation: Net income already includes the revenue, but the cash hasn't been collected, so the increase in AR is subtracted in cash from operations.

blocks.title: How does a gain on an asset sale flow through?
blocks.teaser: Sell equipment with a $100 book value for $120.
blocks.body:
Sell equipment with a $100 book value for $120. IS: $20 gain (net income +$12 at 40% tax). CFS: subtract the $20 gain in CFO (it's not operating cash), then record the full $120 proceeds in CFI. Net cash +$112 (the +$120 proceeds less $8 of tax). BS: cash +$112, PP&E −$100 → assets +$12; equity +$12. Balanced.

**Interview answer:** "Subtract the gain in operating cash flow so it isn't double counted, and show the full proceeds in investing."

blocks.title: D&A is a real economic cost — why add it back?
blocks.teaser: D&A spreads the cost of an asset bought in the past.
blocks.body: D&A spreads the cost of an asset bought in the past. The cash left when the asset was bought (CapEx in CFI). Adding back D&A just prevents counting that cost twice.

blocks.title: What are the most common reasons a model doesn't balance?
blocks.teaser: A CFS line not linked to the BS; a sign flipped in working capital; dividends not deducted from retained earnings; a new BS item with no CFS counterp…
blocks.body: A CFS line not linked to the BS; a sign flipped in working capital; dividends not deducted from retained earnings; a new BS item with no CFS counterpart. Debug by checking the year the imbalance first appears and which line changed.
